VIO-Edge
VIT V-SPACE flight path controller chip · preparation project

VIO-Edge

A drone that trusts only its motion sensors is lost within a minute. This project adds a stereo camera, fuses it with the IMU in a Kalman filter, and then redesigns the vision part the way a flight-controller chip has to run it, down to verified Verilog and silicon area.

Fixed-point front end 0.128 m VIO error on the held-out V1_02 flight
Corner detector RTL bit-exact 356,048 / 356,048 scores per test image
Silicon, SKY130 130 nm 0.182 mm² corner detector logic, one pixel per clock

01

A drone must know where it is, without GPS

A flight controller needs the drone's position, velocity and orientation hundreds of times per second. GPS fails indoors, under bridges and between buildings, and can be jammed. Every drone carries an IMU (a gyroscope and an accelerometer), so the obvious idea is to integrate it: rotation rates give orientation, accelerations give velocity, velocity gives position. This is dead reckoning.

It fails fast. A tiny accelerometer error, integrated twice, grows with the square of time. On the EuRoC V1_01 flight (2.4 minutes, 58 m flown) the IMU-only estimate ends up 91.6 m off on average. A camera fixes this: by watching how the scene moves between two images it measures the drone's motion directly, and that measurement does not drift. Combining the two is visual-inertial odometry (VIO), and with it the error drops to 0.193 m.

The twist is the target: a flight-controller chip. A laptop runs VIO easily. A small, low-power chip needs every stage designed for hardware: integers instead of floating point, streaming instead of random access, fixed latency and as little memory as possible. That redesign, and proof that it still works, is most of this project.

02

The sensors

Gyroscope

Rotation rate on three axes, rad/s. Integrate once for orientation.

Accelerometer

Acceleration minus gravity, in the IMU's own axes. At rest it reads +9.81 m/s² upward.

Bias

A slowly wandering offset on every sample. V1_01's gyro z-bias is 0.076 rad/s: 90° of heading error in 20 s if uncorrected.

EuRoC's drone carries two grayscale cameras, 752×480 pixels at 20 frames per second, mounted 11 cm apart (the baseline). One camera sees how fast things slide across the image but not how far away they are, so it cannot tell 1 m/s past a wall 2 m away from 2 m/s past a wall 4 m away. Two cameras see each point at slightly different horizontal positions. That shift, the disparity, gives metric depth:

Z = f · B / d   =   435 px · 0.110 m / 20 px  =  2.39 m
For the engineer: models and numbers

Pinhole projection u = f·X/Z + cx, v = f·Y/Z + cy; EuRoC uses radial-tangential distortion, undone per point. Rectified focal length 435.2 px, baseline 11.00 cm. IMU: ADIS16448 at 200 Hz, gyro noise 1.7e-4 rad/s/√Hz, accel 2.0e-3 m/s²/√Hz, bias random walks 1.9e-5 rad/s²/√Hz and 3.0e-3 m/s³/√Hz. Depth precision scales as δZ ≈ Z²/(f·B)·δd: at 2.4 m, a 0.1 px disparity error is 1.2 cm.

03

The whole pipeline

Two loops run at different rates. Every IMU sample (200 Hz) the filter predicts by integrating the IMU. Every frame pair (20 Hz) the vision front end measures how the drone moved in the last 50 ms, and the filter corrects itself. The boundary between hardware and software is deliberately narrow: six numbers per frame, a velocity and a rotation rate, plus a quality score.

04

The vision front end, step by step

Step 1 · Find points worth tracking: corners

Slide a small window over the image. On a flat wall, moving it changes nothing. On an edge, you can tell where it is across the edge but not along it (the aperture problem). At a corner, every movement changes the window. Corners are the points whose position can be pinned down, so they are the points worth tracking.

How

Sobel gradients at every pixel; the 2×2 structure tensor of summed gradient products over 3×3; the score is its smaller eigenvalue (Shi-Tomasi). Then grid bucketing: the best corner of every 24×24 cell.

Why this way

Grid bucketing streams (no sort, no second pass) and spreads points evenly, which makes the motion estimate better conditioned.

Considered

Harris: no square root and 9 % less logic, best on the easy flight, but on the faster flight only 73 % of frame pairs worked vs 99.5 %. FAST: cheap but weak gradients for KLT. OpenCV's sort + min-distance: a frame-wide sort.

For the engineer: the score in integers
M = Σ3×3 [gx² gxgy; gxgy gy²] = [a b; b c]    λmin = ((a+c) − √((a−c)² + 4b²)) / 2

Fixed-point: Sobel on 8-bit pixels (±1020) shifted right by 2 to ±255 (9 bits), so each product fits 16 bits; the 3×3 sums are exact 20/21-bit integers; the radicand fits 42 bits and an exact integer square root gives 21 bits. Threshold: 1 % of the previous frame's maximum score (known before the new frame starts, so the hardware never needs two passes).

Step 2 · Follow each point: KLT tracking

A point on a surface keeps nearly the same brightness from one image to the next, so the small window around it should look the same, just shifted. Lucas-Kanade finds that shift: for a small shift the image can be linearised, matching becomes a 2×2 linear system, and solving it repeatedly converges on the shift with sub-pixel precision. It runs twice per frame pair: left to right (stereo) and time t to t+1 (temporal).

Pyramids

The linearisation only holds for a pixel or two, so track first on a quarter-size image (a 20 px shift becomes 5), then refine on half and full size.

Forward-backward check

Track A→B, then B→A. If the point does not come back within 0.5 px, the track is dropped (occlusion, repetitive texture).

Gyro-aided start

The IMU knows how far the camera turned in 50 ms, so tracking starts where rotation alone would put the point.

For the engineer: the iteration and its fixed-point form
G·δ = −b,   G = Σwin ∇A ∇AT,   b = Σwin ∇A · (B(x+d) − A(x)),   d ← d + δ

Chip configuration: 15×15 window, 3 levels, at most 5 iterations (average 3.8), early exit at |δ| < 0.01 px. Scharr gradients in integers (scale 32); bilinear interpolation with 8-bit weights; positions with 8 fractional bits; G and b in 18-bit block floating point (one shared exponent per feature, so the multiplier stays DSP-sized); one reciprocal of det(G) per feature per level with a 16-bit mantissa. Window pixels outside the image are clamped (replicated edge), exactly as a memory read with saturated addresses behaves.

Step 3 · Depth from stereo, without warping the images

The textbook approach first rectifies both images, warping them so that matching points lie on the same row. That needs a full-frame warping unit, a 2.9 MB lookup table and another frame buffer. Here, KLT tracks on the raw camera images, and only the ~200 tracked points are undistorted and rectified, on the CPU at about 60 operations each. A match is kept if both points land on the same row (±1 px) with a disparity between 2 and 120 px.

Step 4 · Motion from points: PnP and RANSAC

Each point now has a 3-D position at time t (from stereo) and a pixel position at t+1 (from tracking). The Perspective-n-Point problem asks which camera motion maps the 3-D points onto the new pixels. RANSAC handles bad tracks: solve from random minimal sets, keep the answer most points agree with (within 1 px), then refine it with all of them. Dividing by the 50 ms gives the velocity and rotation rate; the 7 cm offset between camera and IMU is removed (ω × r). This stays in software: it works on 200 points, not 361,000 pixels.

Result on V1_01: the camera's velocity is accurate to 4.3 cm/s (median) while the drone flies at up to 1 m/s.

05

The filter: trusting each sensor for what it does well

A Kalman filter keeps a best guess of the state and a covariance: how uncertain each part is and how the errors are related. Predict moves the guess forward with the IMU and the uncertainty grows. Correct compares what the camera measured with what the guess says it should have measured, and moves the guess by an amount (the Kalman gain) that depends on which side is more trustworthy. Because errors are linked, correcting velocity also corrects the accelerometer bias, a quantity the camera never measures directly.

Added to the filterWhyEffect
Camera velocity updatethe camera measures motion without drift91.6 → 0.78 m
Exact timing: predict the measurement from the stored path at t₀ and t₁the camera reports the mean over 50 ms; treating it as "now" adds 2.5 cm/s of error, as large as the noisecorrect by construction
Camera as a bias-free gyroscopevelocity cannot reveal the gyro bias; the camera's rotation has none, so the difference is the bias0.78 → 0.193 m
Quality-weighted trustfewer agreeing points or larger reprojection error → less trustrobust
Outlier gate + lock-out guardreject wild measurements, but after 0.5 s of continuous disagreement assume the filter is wrongsafety net
Honest start: ±8.6° tilt uncertainty when the flight does not start stillMH_01 starts hand-held; an over-confident wrong tilt made the filter reject good measurementsMH_01 4.41 → 0.308 m
Camera-confirmed stillnessthe IMU alone cannot see a very gentle take-offWebots 3.18 → 0.081 m
For the engineer: states, Jacobians, noise

Error state δx = [δp, δv, δθ, δba, δbg] (15), local attitude error R = R̂·Exp(δθ); midpoint IMU propagation at 200 Hz (Path Finder ESKF, vendored read-only with checksums).

zv = R(t₀)ᵀ (p(t₁) − p(t₀)) / Δt,   ∂z/∂δv = R₀ᵀ,   ∂z/∂δθ = [ẑ]× R₀ᵀR₁    zω = mean(ωgyro) − bg,   ∂z/∂δbg = −I

Noise σ = 0.03 m/s · √(200 / inliers) · max(1, rms / 0.2 px), calibrated on V1_01 against ground truth (unit-variance normalised error); rotation-rate σ = 0.009 rad/s. χ² gate at 99.9 % (3 dof). IMU noise from the datasheet; a 10× change moves ATE by under 6 mm. Small-lag update (no stochastic cloning): the error state barely changes in 50 ms.

Why loosely coupled: a fixed 15-state filter (~14 k multiply-adds per IMU sample) and a six-number HW/SW interface. Tightly coupled VIO (MSCKF/VINS) reaches 0.05–0.1 m here but grows the state with every remembered frame (O(N³) updates).

06

Redesigning the front end for a chip

A chip is good at doing the same simple operation to a stream of pixels every clock, with fixed timing and a little local memory. It is bad at sorting, unpredictable loops, random access to big memories and, in area and power, floating point. The hardware model reimplements the front end under those rules, in two modes: float measures what the new algorithm costs, fixed adds only quantisation. Every change was measured on its own.

Change from the OpenCV referenceWhy it helps the chipMeasured cost
no full-image rectificationno warp unit, no 2.9 MB table, one fewer frame buffernone
grid bucketingno sort, no second pass, fixed-size outputmore robust: 99.4 % vs 91.8 % of pairs over the full V1_02 flight
at most 5 KLT iterationsfixed worst-case latencynone (average 3.8)
15×15 window, 3 levels2× fewer multiply-adds per iteration, less memorynone
integer pixels, gradients and sumsno floating point in the pixel pathnone
8-bit bilinear weights, 1/256 px positionsnarrow multipliersnone (4-bit weights need 2.4× more iterations)
18-bit block-floating-point solverDSP-sized multiplier, no overflownone (12-bit also fine)

Over the whole V1_01 flight the float and fixed-point versions of the same design give the same VIO error, 0.215 m and 0.215 m: quantisation costs nothing measurable. With the chip configuration, the fixed-point front end tracks 99.4 % of frame pairs on the faster V1_02 flight against 91.8 % for OpenCV, and its median velocity error is 4.22 cm/s against 4.84.

For the engineer: how fixed point and block floating point work

A real number is stored as an integer with an agreed scale: with 8 fractional bits, 3.1416 is stored as round(3.1416 × 256) = 804. Additions are integer additions; a multiplication is followed by a shift. The model logs the largest magnitude every internal signal reaches, which is how the RTL widths were chosen.

In KLT the sums in G and b can need ~45 bits on high-contrast images with large windows, but only their ratio matters. Each feature's G gets one shared exponent: all entries shift right together until they fit 18 bits, and the shift is remembered. b gets its own exponent. δ = G⁻¹b is then rescaled by 2(sb − sG).

07

The RTL block: a streaming corner detector

The corner detector touches every pixel, so it is the highest-rate block, and it does identical work for every pixel with fixed latency. That makes it the right block to prove first in hardware: it can be checked exactly on entire real images. One pixel enters per clock; one score leaves per clock, about 30 clocks later.

Pixels, not gradients

The line buffer keeps 4 rows of 8-bit pixels (24 kbit) and recomputes three Sobel rows. Storing gradients would take 27 kbit and storing the products 81 kbit; two extra Sobel units are far cheaper than SRAM.

Square root, pipelined

One result per clock: 21 stages, each settles one bit. Every stage register is only as wide as that stage needs, which saved 10 % of the area.

Selection on the fly

One register set per cell column keeps the best score and position; when a cell's last pixel is scored, its corner is emitted. No frame buffer, no sort.

Verification: bit-exact on real images

Yosys turns the Verilog into a cycle-accurate C++ simulation (CXXRTL). A testbench streams whole images through it and every output is compared with the Python fixed-point model.

The camera needs only 7.2 Mpixel/s, so a 30 MHz clock already has 4× headroom: speed is not the constraint; area and memory are. The next saving is to share one Sobel unit across three rows over three clocks. These are pre-layout numbers (expect 20–40 % more area after place-and-route); the same RTL goes through Synopsys Design Compiler with a commercial library.

08

What the whole front end costs

The cost model turns the chip configuration and the work measured on real flights (287 features per frame, 3.8 KLT iterations on average) into arithmetic, memory and bandwidth, at 20 frame pairs per second.

ConfigurationM MAC/s (worst)Frame memoryTrafficClock, 16 lanesPairs OKMedian / p99 error
OpenCV-like: 21×21, 4 levels, 10 iterations1492 (2199)1410 KiB253 MB/s196 MHz99.7 %4.39 / 21 cm/s
Chip: 15×15, 3 levels, 5 iterations964 (1052)1395 KiB159 MB/s94 MHz99.5 %4.67 / 24 cm/s
Chip at half resolution617 (708)352 KiB120 MB/s63 MHz99.5 %4.91 / 50 cm/s

Memory is the cost driver. KLT reads windows from the previous left image and the current left and right images, each kept as a 3-level pyramid: 1.4 MB at full resolution, too much SRAM for a small 130 nm chip. Either the images live in external memory (~159 MB/s of traffic) or the front end runs at half resolution: 4× less memory, the same robustness, but twice the tail error. The software side (point rectification, PnP-RANSAC, the filter) needs about 27 MFLOP/s: a microcontroller-class core with an FPU.

09

A simulated drone you can watch

A Webots world (a 14 × 10 m room with generated, feature-rich textures) holds a drone-shaped rig with two forward cameras placed like EuRoC's. It flies a 60 s figure-eight whose tilt obeys quadrotor physics: a multirotor can only push along its own up-axis, so to accelerate by a it must tilt that axis along a + g. The IMU is computed from the same trajectory with the real sensor's noise and a known injected bias, and everything is written in the exact EuRoC format so the unchanged pipeline reads it.

Webots flightValue
Camera velocity error (chip front end, no filter)1.10 cm/s median
Position error: IMU only → VIO (chip front end)2.7 m → 0.077 m
Gyro bias, injected → estimated [rad/s]0.012, -0.020, 0.030 → 0.012, -0.020, 0.030
Accelerometer bias, injected → estimated [m/s²]0.06, -0.09, 0.12 → 0.06, -0.09, 0.12

The simulation is the best case (perfect calibration, no motion blur); EuRoC is the real test. Its value: it found a real filter bug, and it proves the filter recovers a bias it was never told.

Results

Parameters were tuned on V1_01 only; V1_02 (faster, motion blur) and MH_01 (another building, hand-held start) are held out. Error is the RMS position error after aligning the estimate to ground truth (ATE), on a log scale below.

On EuRoC the attitude error stays at 3–8° while in simulation it is 0.24°. No filter setting changes it, and ground truth's own attitude disagrees with the accelerometer's gravity direction by 2.7° while the drone sits still, so part of it comes from the reference and calibration. It is listed as an open item, not explained away.

11

Bugs found, and what they taught

Timestamps rounded by up to 1 sInteger nanoseconds were formatted as floats. Never format integer time as float.
Filter trusted a wrong starting tilt (MH_01)589 good measurements rejected, 4.4 m error. An over-confident filter is worse than an uncertain one.
Zero-velocity updates during a gentle take-off (Webots)1,076 of 1,199 measurements rejected. Let the sensor that can see motion decide when the drone is still.
RTL read the cell table out of range (x ≥ 736)Caught by a simulator assertion. Out-of-range reads are bugs even when the value is ignored.
41·tr² overflowed 42 bits (Harris path)The checkerboard image was off by exactly 2³². Maximum-value stress images belong in every RTL test.
12

Limits and next steps

Limits

Loosely coupled VIO is less accurate than tightly coupled systems. Synthesis is pre-layout with a depth-based clock estimate. Only the corner detector exists in RTL. The Webots rig is kinematic with perfect cameras.

Next in hardware

KLT unit in RTL (patch fetcher + iterative 2×2 solver), verified bit-exact the same way; time-multiplex the corner unit; real SRAM macros and the Synopsys flow for post-layout area, timing and power.

Next in algorithms

Half-resolution front end on more flights; 2-point RANSAC using the gyro's rotation; a tightly coupled (MSCKF) update; a camera at 5 Hz, which matched 20 Hz accuracy on V1_01.

Glossary

ATEabsolute trajectory error: RMS distance between estimated and true positions after aligning the two paths
biasa slowly varying offset added to every IMU sample
bit-exactthe hardware and the model produce identical bits for every output
block floating pointa group of integers sharing one exponent
covariancethe filter's uncertainty, and how its errors are related
disparityhorizontal shift of a point between the left and right images
ESKFerror-state Kalman filter
KLTKanade-Lucas-Tomasi feature tracker
line bufferon-chip memory holding the last few image rows for a streaming filter
MACmultiply-accumulate: one multiplication and one addition
PnP / RANSACcamera motion from 3-D points and their new pixels / robust fitting despite bad data
pyramidthe image at full, half and quarter resolution
RTLregister-transfer level: hardware described in Verilog
VIOvisual-inertial odometry
